summary:
Working with a $1 budget, so writing directly from the notes without extra tool calls.

I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app for myself, and most of the recent work has been finding the places where a drill looked correct but wasn't actually teaching anything. One example: the comprehension check was passing at 88% just by reading the English options, since the four choices differed by a single English word like "where" or "please" — you could get it right without reading a lick of Japanese. I rebuilt the item so the tiles are Japanese and the cue is English, verified the surface-solvable rate drops to zero, and added a second test that checks the fix didn't just break the detector.

I also went down a rabbit hole on image generation. I'm restyling a few hundred illustrations for the app in a manga style, and hit the usual generative-art traps — banning a word in a prompt doesn't remove the thing, it just moves it somewhere else you didn't ban it (a "no leash" prop kept turning into a woman with a leash clipped to her own neck), and negating an object with no negative-prompt support (a different model, Flux) actually draws the thing you named. Fastest fix in both cases was rewording around the concept rather than trying to forbid it.

The other recurring theme has been how bugs propagate when you widen a data structure. I built a feature where a sentence blank could be filled by a two- or three-word phrase instead of a single word, and it quietly broke every downstream piece of code that had been indexing into the old one-word-per-slot format — a blank ended up asking for a character that was still visible elsewhere in the sentence, so there was no correct answer. The fix was a single conversion function that every consumer has to go through now, and a test that sweeps the whole catalog instead of checking one easy case, because the easy case is exactly the one that can't see this class of bug.

Most recently I added actual verb conjugation to the grammar engine — it had been treating every verb form as a fixed string, which caps out fast once you're past beginner-level sentences. Turned out to be cheaper than expected: about a dozen lines of JSON per new grammar rule, no vocabulary re-authoring, because the conjugation logic composes with everything already built rather than needing its own path through the code.

highlights.oneLiner: Restyling a few hundred app illustrations in manga style, chasing prompt-negation traps
